# Feedback

> "for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again"
>
> — Proverbs 24:16

This book has no quarrel with the man in the trap. Its quarrel is with the trap. I'll admit I enjoy the fight, too. Every time a man walks out, I'm glad for the rest of the day.

That gladness comes with some frustration, and nearly all of it is caused by two kinds of reader.

## The man who goes back in {-}

The first is the man who reads the final warning, gets free and finds it easy. A year later he is back where he started, and now it doesn't work for him a second time.

It's like hauling a man out of a river in flood. He lies on the bank coughing and thanking you. Six months later you walk past and he's wading in again.

When you're out, PLEASE DON'T BE THAT MAN.

People assume he went back because he was still hooked and couldn't stand it. That's rarely true. Stopping was so easy that he lost his respect for the trap. He thought, "I could allow myself the odd one. If the worst comes to the worst, I know how to get out again."

It doesn't work like that. Stopping is easy, and controlling it is impossible. The one thing you must do to be free of the habit is not do it.

Men like him have misunderstood the word "easy". So here's a picture.

A man sits on the stone floor of a cold cellar. He's been there so long that he thinks of it as home. In the far wall there's a door with a pane of glass in it. Through the glass he can see a garden with the sun on it. The door isn't locked.

Does it take willpower to stand up and walk out? No. Is leaving any harder than staying? If anything it's easier, because moving warms him up. So why would a man sit on that floor for twenty years? He'd have to have been tricked. Someone would have had to tell him that the garden was dangerous and the floor was comfortable.

All this book does is clean the glass. That's what "easy" means. But an easy door swings both ways. A man who strolls back in "for a minute" will find the floor exactly as cold as he left it, and the glass already misting over.

## The man who won't jump, or jumps and struggles {-}

The second kind is too frightened to try, or tries and finds it a slog. His troubles come under four heads.

### 1. Fear of failure {-}

Failing is no disgrace. Refusing to try is plain foolishness. Look at what you're protecting by not trying. You're protecting nothing. If you try and fail, you're exactly where you are today. If you don't try, you've failed already and saved yourself the bother of hoping.

### 2. Fear of being miserable {-}

Ask the cold question: what dreadful thing will happen to you if you never do this again? The answer is nothing. Go back to Pascal's bet in Chapter 1. All the dreadful things lie the other way.

The panic itself is part of what the habit did to you, and it passes. Being rid of that fear is the best thing you gain. If it rises, breathe slowly. If you're in company and people are grinding you down, step outside. Stand in the garden or the car park for five minutes.

And if you feel like crying, cry. Don't be ashamed of it. We teach boys to clench their jaws and swallow it, and it does them no good. David wept and so did Jesus. If you'd sooner shout, then shout, or go and hit a punchbag. Think of the whole thing as a boxing match you can't lose, because the clock is on your side. Every hour that passes, the Little Monster is weaker. You can't lose, so enjoy the fight.

One serious word. What you feel may be darker than a bad day. If you find yourself thinking about harming yourself, put this book down and talk to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a crisis line. The Appendix lists some. That isn't the Little Monster, and no book is the right tool for it.

And one more, said as gently as I know how. For some men this habit didn't begin with curiosity. It began after something was done to them as children. One therapist was abused himself. He says that most of the men who come to him were too, and that most have never told a soul. If that is part of your story, hear two things. What was done to you was not your sin. And telling someone who knows how to help, a counsellor trained in trauma, is part of getting free. This book can clear away the lies about the habit, but it can't do that work for you. The Appendix says where to start.

### 3. Not following the instructions {-}

You'd be amazed. A man says the method didn't work for him, and then describes how he ignored nearly every instruction in it. He cut down, he kept the folder, he skipped the prayer and he counted days. The instructions are gathered into a checklist that closes this chapter, so that nobody can say he wasn't told.

### 4. Misunderstanding the instructions {-}

These are the commonest ones.

**"I can't stop thinking about it."**

Of course you can't, and you mustn't try. Tell yourself not to think of a white horse and see what trots in. It's like chasing sleep: the harder you try, the wider awake you are. The effort is the problem.

It doesn't matter if the subject crosses your mind fifty times a day. What matters is *what* you think when it does. If you think, "I wish I could," or "When will this end?", you'll be miserable. If you think, "YES! I'M FREE!", you'll be happy fifty times a day.

**"When does the urge die?"**

Nobody can give you a date, and you don't need one. The leftover itch is so faint that you can't tell it from ordinary hunger, tiredness or a flat mood. That's why willpower quitters never know whether they've made it. Months later they feel peckish or fed up, and their mind says, "That's it again. You're owed one."

Think of leaving the dentist with the tooth finally out. Do you sit in the car waiting for your jaw to stop aching before you allow yourself to be relieved? No. Your jaw is sore and you're delighted. The trouble is over and the soreness is only what's left of it.

So don't wait for the urge to die. A man who waits keeps asking, "Is it gone yet? Am I really free if I still feel this?" and those questions produce the fear he was hoping would go away. If a twinge comes, do what one man on a Christian recovery blog does: "Whenever i feel little urge and i pray, i feel completely normal and i also get strength." If you don't pray, say "YES! I'M FREE!" and get on with your day.

**"The moment of revelation hasn't come."**

If you're waiting for it, you're building another phobia.

Years ago, on one of my willpower attempts, I got to three weeks. I ran into an old friend, the only one who knew, and he asked how it was going. "I've survived three weeks," I said.

"Survived? What do you mean, survived?"

"I've gone three weeks without."

"And what's the plan? Survive till you're ninety? What are you waiting for? You've done it. You're a man who doesn't do that."

I thought, "He's right. What *am* I waiting for?" I didn't understand the trap in those days, and I was soon back in it. But I never forgot the point. You were free when you said Amen. The only job left is to be happy about it from the start.

**"I still want it."**

Then you're contradicting yourself. You can't say, "I want to be a man who's free of this," and in the next breath, "I want to do it." A man who's free doesn't want to. You already know which man you want to be, so stop tormenting yourself with the other one's lines.

**"I feel as if I've stopped living."**

Why? Nobody asked you to. For a week or two you'll have a slight disturbance in the background: a faint, almost unnoticeable itch. Now think. You've had that itch for years, every hour you weren't feeding it. You had it in church, at work, at your mother's table and all night while you slept, and it never spoiled a meal. If you hadn't stopped, you'd have carried it to the grave.

The habit never added to a single occasion. It took from them. So go to the party and the wedding and the beach. Stay late and enjoy your dinner. Don't envy the smooth operator across the room with his three phone numbers. If he goes home alone to what you've left behind, he'd change places with you. You're not the one going without.

**"I'm miserable and irritable."**

Then you've missed an instruction. Find out which one. Some men understand every word of this book and believe it, and still set off like a man walking to the gallows. But you're doing the thing you most wanted to do, and what every man in the trap wishes he could do. Whatever method a man uses, the goal is a frame of mind in which every thought of the habit ends with "YES! I'M FREE!" If that's where you want to finish, why not begin there? Start in that frame of mind and stay in it. There's no other way.

**"I fell. Am I back to zero?"**

There's no counter in this book, so there's no zero to go back to. Your freedom was never a number. A man in a recovery group pictured it as a row of hurdles: "you cleanly got over ten and then you kind of stumbled on like the 11th but that doesn't mean that you've fallen over and you have to start again".

But don't shrug it off. Something real happened. You fed the Little Monster and your conscience knows it. So do three things, in this order.

*Confess it today.* Don't wait until you've punished yourself for a week. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful": you learned that in Chapter 20, and it wasn't only for the first time. Solomon didn't say the righteous man never falls. He said he gets up, seven times if he must. C.S. Lewis put it this way: "The only fatal thing is to sit down content with anything less than perfection". Sitting down is the fatal part. A fall needn't be. One young man put it in a line worth keeping: "You are not your past you are how you respond to your past". And remember the two words from the last chapter, spoken to a man who still smelled of yesterday: just come.

*Refuse the second one.* The real danger was never the fall. It's the thought that arrives an hour later: "Well, I've blown it now, so I may as well." That's the streak counter talking. One fall is a fall, and a week of "may as well" puts you back inside. The pang is made of fear. A man who decides he's "hooked for life" after one slip has scared himself into the cellar.

*Find the instruction you broke.* A fall is always a failure to follow one of them. You doubted, or you waited, or you kept a substitute, or you "tested" yourself, or you'd kept a way back. The things you learned in this book haven't been unlearned. Find the gap, re-read that chapter, pray the prayer again and be glad again. You fell forward.

**"Should I tell my wife or my pastor?"**

Chapter 15 said secrecy is this habit's power and promised an answer here. You've already told God, and that's the confession that counts most. As for people, here's what I'd do.

*Tell one man.* A pastor, an elder, or an older friend with some sense. James tells believers to confess to one another and pray for one another, and there's a reason. A thing that's been said out loud to another man loses half its size. A Christian writer on the subject says, "If you want to quit a habit, then get accountable".

But be clear what you're asking him for. You're not hiring a policeman. A weekly "did you or didn't you" is the Willpower Method with a witness, and it keeps the subject at the centre of your life. Tell him as a free man giving news: "This had me for years. It's over. I wanted one person to know." Then let him ask whenever he likes.

*Your wife.* I think a marriage is better with no locked rooms in it, so in general, yes, and in good time. But ask yourself what you're after. If you want to unload your guilt onto her so that *you* feel lighter, wait. That's using her again. Tell her when you can do it for her sake: plainly, without gory detail, and without asking her to keep score. She isn't your parole officer. There may be more behind it: porn, another woman, or anything worse. If so, talk to your pastor or a Christian counsellor first about how to tell her well.

*Nobody else needs to know.* Chapter 19 told you not to post "Day 1" anywhere, and that still stands. You don't need an audience.

## The Checklist {-}

Follow these and you cannot fail.

1. **You've made your vow. Keep it.** That means never again, and it covers the hand, edging, "just touching", porn "instead" and the scroll that's lust with the sound off.
2. **Be clear that there is nothing to give up.** I don't mean that you're better off without it. You always knew that. I don't mean that it's irrational but still gives you some comfort. I mean there is no real pleasure or support in it at all. It's an illusion, like holding your breath for the joy of breathing again.
3. **There's no such thing as a hopeless case.** You aren't built differently. You're one of millions of men who walked into a clever trap, and like the many who once thought they'd never get out, you're out.
4. **Weigh it up on any day of your life and the answer is the same:** don't. Nothing will ever change that. You've made the right decision, so never torture yourself by doubting it.
5. **Don't try not to think about it,** and don't fret if you think about it a lot. Each time you do, today or in thirty years, think: "YES! I'M FREE!"
6. **Use no substitutes.** Don't set yourself dares, like the phone on the pillow at midnight. Don't build a fortress either, hiding from films, beaches and women. Change nothing in your life simply because you've stopped.
7. **Don't wait for the moment of revelation.** Get on with living. Enjoy the good days and cope with the bad ones, and it will arrive before you've noticed.

A man who can't control his lust can't be trusted. Keep these seven and you'll be a man who can.

## More questions {-}

**"I had a wet dream. Does it count?"**

No. Chapter 21 covered this. A dream is not a decision. One recovery site says it plainly: "Normal bodily functions cannot be viewed as a relapse." And if you're worried about your health, the Cleveland Clinic says of wet dreams, "They don't mean anything is wrong." You've nothing to confess and nothing to undo. If you wake up aroused, you don't have to do anything about it. Get up, change the sheets and have breakfast.

**"My body doesn't work properly with my wife. How long until it does?"**

Chapter 8 described this. The honest answer is that nobody can give you a date. The medical student in that chapter was well in a little over a month. One recovery coach went through it himself. He says it was about two and a half months before things worked at all, and another six of gradual progress after that. A few men report longer. The sex therapist who has written most about it tells his patients, again and again, that the restraint he asks of them is "only temporary".

So be patient with your body, and tell your wife what is going on, because the worst part for her is thinking it's her fault. See a doctor too, since medicines and other conditions can cause the same trouble. And don't "test" things on your own in the meantime. You know what that is.

**"I can't sleep without it. Should I sort out my sleep first?"**

No. Carry on with the book and with your freedom, and let sleep catch up. Chapter 5 took the "sleeping pill" apart: it never gave you rest, it only knocked you flat. You may have two or three nights of lying awake while the old bedtime cue wears off. They're not an emergency. Lie there and be glad.

Meanwhile do the ordinary, sensible things. Go to bed at the same time each night and keep the phone out of the bedroom. You don't need a special programme. The psalm says of God that "he gives sleep to his loved ones", and you'll find that sleep comes more easily to a man with nothing on his conscience.
